title: Fort Dearborn, summer 1812

lighting.note: Mid-afternoon, 14 August 1812, the eve of the evacuation, in local mean solar time at the datum: the renderer's solar position puts the sun 43 degrees up at azimuth 247 (west-south-west), against 46 degrees at azimuth 250 on the 1 August the scene was first dated, so the light the view was chosen for still holds. Chosen for the view the scene opens on: the visitor stands south-west of the fort facing north-east, so a sun in the south-west lights the south and west faces of the picket rows and the south-west blockhouse corner they see first, rather than leaving the fort in its own shadow as a morning sun would.

note: The 1812 scene (T-2050, piece 3 of T-0469): the first Fort Dearborn on its natural ground on 14 August 1812, the eve of the evacuation of the 15th and the burning of the 16th. THE DATE IS THE OWNER'S (2026-10-13, T-2490, moved by T-2514): the scene was first dated 1 August, and moves to the 14th so that the camp of the August gathering, assembled by the council of the 12th (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII), stands on the scene date; the card `the_eve` says what the day was, and stages nothing of it. It resolves the fourteen first_fort_dearborn_* records (phase first_fort_1803, 1803-08-17..1812-08-16), the eleven first_fort_outer_* records outside the stockade (T-2062, T-2507), and, across the river, the Kinzie house and its fenced green (kinzie_house_1812 and kinzie_house_1812_green, phase kinzie_1804, 1804-10-01..1833-12-31, T-2497), the Kinzie establishment behind the house - its stable, lodging house for the Frenchmen, bake-house, dairy and picket garden (kinzie_stable_1812, kinzie_lodging_house_1812, kinzie_bake_house_1812, kinzie_dairy_1812 and kinzie_garden_1812, phase kinzie_1804) and Whistler's old horse mill west of it (kinzie_horse_mill_1812, phase mill_1808, 1808-01-25..1816-06-30), T-2485, L420, and Antoine Ouilmette's house, the draught's third no. 31 house, nearest the Kinzie house and a little behind it (ouilmette_house_1812, phase ouilmette_1812, 1808-01-25..1829-12-31, review_required and touches_removal, T-2486, L-1812-ouilmette-2486), with the camera `kinzie_yard` east-north-east of the yard looking across it to the house, about where Eastman's view of 1820 was drawn from; the camp of the August gathering, three groups of mat lodges on the banks of the State Street creek (potawatomi_camp_1812_mouth, _middle and _upper, phase camp_1812, 1812-08-12..1812-08-16, review_required and touches_removal, T-2515, L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515; the card `the_camp`, and the camera `potawatomi_camp`, 22 m above the bank at the creek's mouth looking south-west up it, raised because the prairie stands taller than eye height between the bank and the lodges), and nothing of 1835: every other record's phases open later, and the second fort's open on 1816-07-01, so no date can draw the two forts together - tools/read_whistler_1808.py --check holds both of those. It stands on e1830_natural, the pre-cut mouth with the river turned south behind the baymouth spit (T-2002, T-2003). The fort is seated with one origin and one bearing: the draught's staff foot on the fort site at local E +1152, N +221, the frame's north on grid north (each record's position note says why). THE SPAWN IS A CAMERA, NOT A CLAIM: 57 m south-west of the staff, outside both picket rows, facing it. `first_fort_gate` stands 25 m south of the staff, 8 m outside the outward row, on the line of the main gate's passage (E -11.1..-4.9 ft in the fort's frame). THE COVER (T-0471): the flora layer is drawn, and data/flora/index.json's `scenes` lists decide what of it stands here - the natural zone records (prairie, sedge meadow, marsh, river timber, wet woods, beach and sand prairie) are the ground's and are dealt from this epoch's heightfield, while the settled town's sward and the 1835 plantings (dooryards, the Lombardy rows, the Sauganash's trees, the willows by the second fort) are scoped to 1835 and stand nowhere here. The plantings of this scene are massacre_cottonwoods_1812, a remembered pair whose existence is inferred and whose places are reconstructed (L372), and kinzie_house_1812_trees, the Kinzie house's four Lombardy poplars and its two cottonwoods (T-2497, L-kinzie-house-1812-2497), and ouilmette_garden_1812, the currant bushes behind Antoine Ouilmette's house (T-2486, L-1812-ouilmette-2486); the cover's own month and the garrison's missing clearing are L371. The other town-wide layers written for 1835 are still left out - fauna, streets, enclosures and the rest are dated 1 July 1835 and none of them is true here. `kinzie_house_across_river` stands on the fort's mound 12 m north of its outward picket row and looks north across the river at the Kinzie house, the view Lossing's engraving takes. `eighteenth_street_shore` is a CAMERA on the conjectural bank three kilometres south of the fort, looking east-south-east at the two cottonwoods; it does not locate the battle, which is T-0470's to map. `lees_place_reach` is a CAMERA on T-2501's ruled reach of the South Branch's north-west bank, 930 m west of the box: it stands on the apron field `terrain_apron` names (T-2502), the 1812 ground carried down the river from the box floor at the conjectural grade, and looks south-east across the channel. It marks the reading's station, and since T-2509 stands 6 m back from it on the bank top, between the water and the field's fence (it stood 20 m back until the fence enclosed that point): `lees_place_cabin_1812` 30 m back from that station with its river front to the channel, inside the worm fence of `lees_place_field_fence_1812`. `lees_place_cabin` is a CAMERA on the opposite (south-east) bank, 94 m from the cabin and a little upstream of it, looking north across the river at its front and its upstream gable, the side the 1912 plate draws; it claims nothing about where anyone stood. The card `where_lees_place_stood` gives the four placings and where they disagree. No person is drawn: the Indigenous-history review gates of T-0472 come before any figure. The scene's cards (T-0472) name the event, say whose accounts it rests on and where they disagree, and are held for that review, so this scene is not released. THE EXCLUSIONS LAYER (T-2489) is this scene's own: data/exclusions.json entries whose `scenes` names 1812 are the structures the record places at Chicago before the evacuation that were researched and ruled out of this date, and the 1835 town's entries, which carry no `scenes`, are not listed here (tools/exclusion_scope.py).

cards.title: The fort you see, and the plan it is built from
cards.text: This is the first Fort Dearborn, built in 1803 and burned on 16 August 1812, the morning after its garrison marched out. It is built from the only known plan of it: the draught Captain John Whistler drew of his own post in January 1808. The plan states its own scale for the garrison and for nothing outside the stockade, and it gives no reliable height, so the buildings' heights are this project's reading and not Whistler's. The second fort, begun in 1816 on the same site, is not drawn in this year.

quotes.cite: Captain Nathan Heald, 1812, as printed in Moses and Kirkland's History of Chicago (1895), p. 50

cards.confidence_note: The plan, its date and its scale are Whistler's own (tier 1); the burning is the commanding officer's own letter, read as quoted in the 1895 history's machine OCR ('tire' and 'wilh' read as 'fire' and 'with'). That the heights are not Whistler's is the source record's own finding: the folded elevations on the sheet disagree with one another.

cards.title: The day you see: 14 August 1812, the eve of the evacuation
cards.text: This scene shows the afternoon of 14 August 1812. The order to evacuate the fort had been read on parade days before. The Potawatomi of the neighbouring villages had come in, as the commanding officer wrote, 'from all quarters', and were camped on the south bank of the river; a council had been held with them on the 12th, the factory's goods were given out on the 13th, and the arms and liquor the garrison could not carry were destroyed. The garrison and the families with it marched out the next morning. Nothing of that day is staged here: no one is drawn. The camp's lodges stand empty on the creek west of the fort (see 'The camp on the creek').

cards.confidence_note: The council of the 12th, the order read on parade, the march 'on the following morning' and the encampment on the south bank are Wau-Bun's, a family narrative printed forty-four years after the event; the goods given out on the 13th and the arms and liquor destroyed are Wau-Bun's as quoted in the 1895 history (p. 48, lines 7328-7341). Heald's letter, written within months, agrees that the neighbouring Indians came in for the goods, but it dates Captain Wells's arrival, which Wau-Bun puts on the 14th and makes the day the march was settled, to the 13th (p. 48, line 7397), so the day-by-day order of the 13th and 14th is Wau-Bun's and not the commanding officer's. Heald's letter is read in that history's machine OCR (';is' read as 'as').
cards.review_note: Held for review because this card describes the Potawatomi gathering and encampment before the attack of 15 August from accounts written by the garrison's side and a settler family, and how that gathering is told is the Indigenous-history judgement AGENTS.md places under consultation with Native scholars or community organisations before the scene is released.

cards.title: The camp on the creek: the Potawatomi lodges of August 1812
cards.text: West of the fort, on the south bank of the river, three groups of lodges stand along the creek that ran into the river at the later State Street. The accounts put the camp of the August gathering there: the Potawatomi of the neighbouring villages had come in, a council was held with them on the 12th, and on the evening of the 14th the lodges stood 'clustered along the creek'. Lodges of this region and these years were covered with rush mats on a frame of bent poles, with a smoke opening at the top and a mat over the door, and that is how they are drawn. What is reconstructed: the number (26, far fewer than a gathering of hundreds of families would have needed), where each group stands on the bank, and every lodge's shape and size. No one is drawn and nothing is staged; the lodges stand empty.

The lodge's covering and frame are read from Wau-Bun's description of a lodge in 1831, not of this camp. The count, the three grounds and the lodge's shape and size are this project's (L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515). Footnote 36 of Wau-Bun puts the stream 'Along the present State Street'.
cards.review_note: Held for review because this card and the lodges it describes reconstruct the camp of the Potawatomi gathered at Chicago before the attack of 15 August 1812, from accounts written by the garrison's side and settler historians, and how that camp is shown is the Indigenous-history judgement AGENTS.md places under consultation with Native scholars or community organisations before the scene is released.

cards.title: What the event of 15 August 1812 is called
cards.text: The morning after the afternoon this scene shows, on 15 August 1812, the garrison and the families with it left the fort under orders to march to Fort Wayne, and their column was attacked on the lake shore south of the river mouth by warriors Captain Heald counted as mostly Potawatomi. It is called both the Battle of Fort Dearborn and the Fort Dearborn Massacre, and choosing between the names is a judgement about the event. The sources split the same way from the start: the commanding officer wrote of 'the action'; the 1895 history heads its chapter 'The Massacre'. This reconstruction takes neither name as its verdict, and calls it the evacuation of the fort and the attack on the lake shore.

Heald's letter is read as quoted in that history's machine OCR, so it is graded no higher than the compilation it reaches us through.

cards.title: Where the attack happened: two answers that do not meet
cards.text: The accounts place the attack in two ways, and they do not agree. Captain Heald, writing within weeks, measured it along the march: about a mile and a half from the fort, at a bank between the beach and the prairie. A later tradition, written down in the 1880s and 1890s, pointed to two old cottonwoods left standing in Eighteenth Street and called them the Massacre trees. Eighteenth Street is about two miles and an eighth from the fort site in a straight line, farther than a mile and a half reaches before the march's bends are counted. The two cottonwoods stand in this scene where that tradition put them, as a tradition and not as a marker. This reconstruction does not choose between the two answers, and nothing in it marks where the attack happened.

quotes.locator: p. 50, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 7586-7588, Heald's letter (the OCR's 'bad' and 'hall' read as 'had' and 'half')
quotes.cite: Captain Nathan Heald, 1812, as printed in Moses and Kirkland's History of Chicago (1895), p. 50
quotes.text: We had proceeded about a mile and a half when it was discovered that the Indians were preparing to attack us from behind the bank.

quotes.locator: p. 60, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 8886-8892
quotes.cite: Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago (1895), p. 60
quotes.text: When Eighteenth street came to be laid out there stood between its curb stones, two old cottonwood trees which were pointed out by earlier traditions as marking the battle-ground and named the "Massacre trees,"

cards.confidence_note: Both placings are documented as statements; neither is adopted. The straight-line distance is this project's measurement in the local frame: the first fort's flagstaff foot at E +1152, N +221 (this scene's note) to the OpenStreetMap crossing of 18th Street and Prairie Avenue at E +1401.9, N -3206.9 (data/traces/south_anchor_control.json § control.eighteenth_prairie), 3,437 m or 2.14 miles. The march went down the river before it reached the beach, so its length to that crossing is longer still. Where a mile and a half falls on the 1812 shore is derived in data/terrain/1812_evacuation_route.geojson (T-0470) and is not drawn here; the cottonwoods are the planting massacre_cottonwoods_1812 (T-0471), whose existence is inferred from the same tradition and whose places are reconstructed (L372).
cards.review_note: Held for review because this card locates a battle fought by Potawatomi and allied warriors from accounts written by the garrison's side and by settler historians, which is the Indigenous-history review AGENTS.md requires before the scene is released.

cards.title: Whose accounts these are
cards.text: Every account this scene reads was written by the garrison's side or by settler historians: Captain Heald's letter, his son's recollection printed in 1881, the 1895 history that quotes them both, and Quaife's study of 1913. None was written by the Potawatomi, and the 1895 history tells the event in its own era's terms. One Native statement reaches the record, and only at second hand, through a settler's daughter half a century later. A fuller account needs Potawatomi history and Native scholarship that this project has not yet read; the Newberry Library's Indigenous Chicago materials are where that reading begins.

cards.title: Where Lee's Place stood: four placings that do not all meet
cards.text: Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch, later called Hardscrabble, is placed four ways, and they do not all agree. Captain Heald, writing nine days after two of Lee's men were killed there in April 1812, put the cabin about three miles from the garrison. Gurdon Hubbard, who knew the place from 1818, put the same premises half a mile below Bridgeport on the river's north side. The 1895 history put it on the north-western side of the branch near its forks. Currey in 1912 put it at the canal's mouth itself, half a mile higher than Hubbard, and four miles from the river's mouth, which by the river's course falls about a mile short of both. This scene stands the cabin where Hubbard's half mile falls, on the north-west bank that every placing naming a side agrees on; Heald's three miles and the forks fit it, and Currey's two placings do not.

cards.title: Why no one is drawn here
cards.text: This scene shows the fort, the houses and the lodges on their ground, and nothing else. No soldier, family or Potawatomi person is drawn - not the garrison's daily life, not the march, not the attack - and none will be until Native scholars or community organisations have reviewed how this event is shown. The cards above are held for that review, so the scene is not released. An empty, accurate fort is honest; a populated, invented one is not.
